questions.q: What is the dividing line between artificial intelligence and machine learning, and how are the two related?
keyPoints: AI is the goal: building systems that behave intelligently (reason, perceive, decide); ML is one way to achieve it
ML is a subset of AI, so every ML system is AI but not every AI system is ML
The dividing line is learning: AI may use rules a human wrote, whereas ML learns patterns from data
questions.explanation: A rule-based expert system is AI but not ML because it never learns.

questions.q: How does robotic process automation (RPA) differ from business process automation (BPA)?
keyPoints: RPA is task-level: a software bot mimics a human at the user interface to automate one repetitive task, leaving the process unchanged
BPA is process-level: it orchestrates and often redesigns a whole end-to-end workflow, integrating systems directly with approvals and an audit trail
Keyword: RPA is a robot doing a task; BPA is redesigning a process

questions.q: How does machine learning enhance a rule-based automation workflow like invoice processing?
keyPoints: Plain rule-based automation only handles structured, predictable input and breaks on anything needing judgement
ML adds intelligence at decision points: classifying document type, extracting fields from varied layouts, detecting anomalies
Effect: the workflow copes with unstructured input and exceptions, raising the share of cases handled without a human
questions.explanation: Automation provides the hands; ML provides the eyes and judgement.

questions.q: How do supervised and unsupervised learning differ?
keyPoints: Supervised trains on labelled data (each input paired with the correct answer) and learns to predict a known output for new inputs
Unsupervised trains on unlabelled data and discovers hidden structure, such as natural groupings (clustering)
The deciding question is simply: do you have labels?

questions.q: Why is reinforcement learning not just a form of supervised learning?
keyPoints: Supervised learning is given the correct answer for every example up front, as a fixed answer key
Reinforcement learning has no answer key: an agent acts in an environment and only gets a reward or penalty after acting
A reward tells the agent how good the outcome was, never what the right action would have been

questions.q: How does a decision tree make a prediction, and why is that valuable?
keyPoints: It asks a sequence of test questions about the input, following the branch that matches each answer from the root down to a leaf
The leaf gives the final prediction; the questions and their order are learned from data, not hand-written
You can state the exact path of answers that produced the prediction, making the tree interpretable

questions.q: What does a single neuron in a neural network compute?
keyPoints: It multiplies each input by a weight and adds them up (with a bias) to form a weighted sum
It passes that sum through an activation function to produce its output
Weights say how much each input matters and are the learned parameters; a network is layers of these joined by weighted connections

questions.q: Why does explainability matter when comparing decision trees and neural networks?
keyPoints: A decision tree is interpretable: you can trace the path and say exactly why it decided; a neural network is a black box whose decision is spread across many weights
The trade-off is transparency versus power: trees are explainable but weaker on complex tasks, networks are powerful but opaque
Explainability underpins accountability and lets you audit a model for bias, so interpretable models are often preferred for high-stakes decisions

questions.q: Why is RPA considered brittle, and what causes it?
keyPoints: An RPA bot works through the user interface, locating fields and buttons by position or label the way a human would
When the application is updated (a moved button, renamed field, new step) the bot can no longer find what it expects and fails
Because it mimics a human at the screen rather than talking to a stable API, it needs ongoing maintenance and is not a permanent fix

questions.q: What is the key difference between linear and logistic regression?
keyPoints: Linear regression predicts a continuous number by fitting a straight line (e.g. a house price)
Logistic regression, despite its name, performs classification: it predicts a category/yes-or-no
It uses the sigmoid function to output a probability between 0 and 1, then thresholds it into a class
questions.explanation: Linear predicts a number; logistic predicts a yes-or-no.

questions.q: What is overfitting, and why must you evaluate a model on a separate test set?
keyPoints: Overfitting is when a model fits the training data too closely, memorising its noise rather than the general pattern, so it fails on new data
A model can memorise its training data, so a high training score proves nothing about real performance
A train-test split evaluates on unseen data; a big gap between high training and low test accuracy reveals overfitting

questions.q: In plain terms, how does a neural network learn from data?
keyPoints: It repeats a cycle of Predict, Loss, Adjust over many passes (epochs) of the training data
Predict: run a forward pass to get an output; Loss: measure how far it is from the known correct label
Adjust: nudge every weight to reduce the error (via backpropagation and gradient descent), so predictions get closer over time

questions.q: Why is it wrong to claim a machine learning model is 'neutral' or 'objective'?
keyPoints: The maths is impartial, but the model faithfully learns the patterns in its training data
That data is generated by humans and the real world, which carry biases and inequities, so the model mirrors and can amplify them
Bias appears even when no one intends it and even when the sensitive attribute is not a direct input
questions.explanation: Amazon's recruiting model penalised resumes mentioning 'women's' because it learned a male-dominated hiring history.

questions.q: How does historical bias enter a machine learning system, and why doesn't more data fix it?
keyPoints: Historical bias occurs when the data accurately records a past that was itself unequal, so the model learns and perpetuates that discrimination
The data isn't 'wrong' — it is a faithful record of an unjust history, which the model reproduces
Collecting more of the same biased history just deepens the bias; you need contemporary, balanced, or corrected data

questions.q: Why does forecasting sometimes fail badly, even when the model was accurate on past data?
keyPoints: Forecasting (supervised regression) assumes the future will resemble the training data
When conditions shift into patterns the model never saw, its predictions can be systematically wrong
So forecasts need human oversight and confidence limits, not blind trust
questions.explanation: Zillow's price model overpaid for thousands of homes when the market shifted, losing hundreds of millions.

questions.q: Why can a model with high overall accuracy still be unfair, and how is bias mitigated?
keyPoints: Overall accuracy can be high while the model performs badly for a minority group, because the average hides the gap
You must measure fairness per group (e.g. demographic parity or equalised odds), not just overall accuracy
Mitigate across the pipeline: diverse/representative data at the source, reweighting under-represented groups in training, and fairness metrics after

questions.q: How can patterns in human behaviour, such as acute stress, distort a machine learning system?
keyPoints: Under acute stress people are rushed, less accurate, and inconsistent, so their input differs from calm data
A model trained only on calm 'happy-path' data performs worst exactly when users are most stressed and need it most
Fix: train on data reflecting realistic high-pressure use and design interfaces that detect stress and adapt
questions.explanation: A diagnosis assistant trained on unhurried inputs can fail an exhausted doctor at 3am.
